questions.subtopic: 1C6 Risk management across the organization. A process that runs but is not used
questions.question: A Kazakh logistics group's units rate risks on one approved scale and escalate them as required, and its major investment papers do not mention risk. Which conclusion by internal auditor Dana Akhmetova is MOST accurate?

options.A: Effective: ratings and escalation both follow the approved method
options.B: Effective: internal audit assesses the process, not managers' business decisions
options.C: Not effective: risk management is judged by use, not by ratings alone
options.D: Not effective: major investments need the risk function's approval first

questions.key_concept: Assessing risk management covers design, operation and use: a process that runs as designed is not fully effective until risk information shapes decisions.
questions.pre_read: Three questions: is the process well set up, is it followed, and does anyone decide differently because of it?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management describes assurance over it as covering whether risks are identified, assessed and escalated reliably and also whether decision-makers use the risk information. Here the first parts work, but major investment decisions are made without reference to risk. The closest choice stops at ratings and escalation: a process that is followed yet changes no decision has not done its job.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: sound ratings and escalation show the process is followed. Effectiveness also asks whether risk information is used, and the investment papers suggest it is not.
wrong_explanations.B: True as far as it goes: the decisions are management's. But whether risk information feeds them is part of the process that assurance over risk management evaluates.
wrong_explanations.D: Management decides on investments; the risk function supports and challenges. The gap is that the papers ignore risk information, not that an approval is missing.

tips: Eliminate: B, because whether decisions use risk information is part of the process being assessed, and D, because the risk function challenges while management decides.
Final two: C beats A because following the method shows the process operates; with no investment paper mentioning risk, its output is not used where decisions are made.
Exam cue: for risk management, check design, operation and use. A register kept perfectly that no decision refers to is a record, not risk management.

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. A control with no written procedure
questions.question: A Welsh joinery has no written procedures, but its owner inspects every order before dispatch and notes each inspection on the job card. How should internal auditor Rhys Morgan BEST regard the inspection?

options.A: As a control to assess: the job cards show whether inspections happen
options.B: As no control yet: nothing written obliges the owner to keep inspecting
options.C: As a design-stage control: without a procedure, its operation is untestable
options.D: As a control already proven: every job card carries the owner's note

questions.key_concept: A control is any action taken to manage risk. An unwritten practice is still a control, and its design and operation can be assessed.
questions.pre_read: Ask what makes something a control: the paper that describes it, or what is actually done about a risk?
questions.correct_explanation: In the Standards' glossary a control is defined by what is done: any action, whoever takes it, that manages risk and helps objectives be met. The owner's inspection is such an action, and the job cards give evidence of whether it happens, so Rhys can assess its design and operation. The closest choice assumes nothing can be tested without a written procedure, but Standard 13.4's considerations accept undocumented procedures as criteria.

wrong_explanations.B: A control is the action taken, not the document that requires it. The inspection manages the risk of faulty orders now; writing it down can still be recommended.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: an unwritten practice can still be tested. The established practice serves as the criterion, and the job cards and observation show whether it is carried out.
wrong_explanations.D: A note on a job card is evidence to examine, not proof. Whether the inspection would catch faults, and whether the notes are reliable, still has to be assessed.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a control is the action taken and not the document requiring it, and D, because a note on a job card is evidence to test, not proof.
Final two: A beats C because an unwritten practice can serve as the criterion, and the job cards let Rhys test whether the inspection is carried out.
Exam cue: do not confuse a control with its documentation. Look first for what people actually do about the risk, then ask whether it is written down.

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. Dropping a detective control beside a preventive one
questions.question: A Maltese insurer's supervisors may override its payment-limit block and did 42 times; the claims manager proposes dropping the monthly review that alone checks overrides. Which view by internal auditor Marija Borg is MOST accurate?

options.A: Sound: overrides are supervisors' decisions, so review adds little
options.B: Unsound: authority to override is itself a risk that needs a control
options.C: Sound: a control that duplicates another is a cost worth removing
options.D: Unsound: a review after payment should be replaced by one before it

questions.key_concept: Control types do different jobs. Where a preventive control can be overridden, the detective control that reviews overrides is the remaining check on that route.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each control covers, and which payments would be left with no control if the review went.
questions.correct_explanation: A preventive control acts before the event and a detective control reveals it afterward; Standard 13.2's considerations name both types. The block stops a payment only until a supervisor overrides it, so the power to override is a risk of its own, and dropping the monthly review would leave it with no control. The closest choice wants the check moved before payment, a design preference these facts do not establish.

wrong_explanations.A: A supervisor's override is the event that needs a second look, not a check on itself. The review is the only scrutiny those 42 payments get.
wrong_explanations.C: Removing a duplicate control can be right, but nothing here is duplicated: the review covers the payments the block lets through on override.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: an earlier check might be stronger, but that is a design choice for management. The proposal is unsound because overrides would have no check at all.

tips: Eliminate: A, because an override needs a second look and is not a check on itself, and C, because the review duplicates nothing: it covers what the block lets through.
Final two: B beats D because timing is not the issue; without the review, the authority to override would have no control over it.
Exam cue: before agreeing that a control is redundant, list what each control covers. If one route is covered by a single control, that control is not spare.

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. Management prefers a different fix
questions.question: Internal auditor Kemal Aydin recommended that a Turkish hospital lock dose limits into its infusion pumps; the nursing manager prefers a second-nurse check that Kemal agrees stops the same errors. What is Kemal's BEST course?

options.A: Hold to the lock and record the manager's disagreement
options.B: Hold to the lock and take it to the chief audit executive
options.C: Accept the manager's action and withdraw the finding from the results
options.D: Accept the manager's action and track it until it is in place

questions.key_concept: Actions on a finding are agreed with management, which may choose its own remedy; the auditor then confirms that the agreed action was implemented.
questions.pre_read: Whose decision is the remedy, and what does the auditor still owe once a remedy is agreed?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.4 lets internal auditors develop recommendations, ask for action plans or agree on actions with management, and leaves implementation to management, so a different remedy that deals with the same cause is acceptable. Standard 15.2 has internal auditors confirm the action was implemented, and its considerations have a satisfactory alternative plan tracked to completion. Withdrawing the finding, the closest choice, forgets that the gap existed and that a plan is not yet a control.

wrong_explanations.A: Recording both positions is for a disagreement that discussion cannot resolve. Kemal agrees the manager's action works, so nothing is in dispute.
wrong_explanations.B: The chief audit executive helps resolve results that auditor and management cannot agree on. Here they agree on an action that deals with the cause.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: accepting the alternative is right, but the gap existed. The finding stays in the results with the agreed action, and internal auditors confirm it is implemented.

tips: Eliminate: A, because both positions are recorded only when a disagreement remains, and B, because the chief audit executive steps in when the parties cannot agree.
Final two: D beats C because an agreed action does not erase the finding; it is reported with the action, and internal auditors confirm it was implemented.
Exam cue: the auditor's recommendation is one route, not the only one. Accept a management action that deals with the root cause, then follow it to completion.

questions.subtopic: 1C8 Control design, effectiveness and efficiency. Choosing which controls to test
questions.question: Planning a payroll engagement at a Senegalese port, internal auditor Awa Diop judged one key control's design adequate and another's inadequate; both address significant risks. Which plan for testing operating effectiveness fits BEST?

options.A: Test both controls: each conclusion needs evidence of how it operates
options.B: Test the weak control first: testing should follow the higher risk
options.C: Test the sound control: the weak design is already a finding
options.D: Test neither yet: a design finding is first agreed with management

questions.key_concept: Design is usually judged before operation is tested. A sound design is worth testing; an inadequate one is already a potential finding.
questions.pre_read: For each control ask what a test of operation could add to what the design review already showed.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.2's considerations note that fully testing controls that are not adequately designed is unlikely to be worth the cost, and those of Standard 13.2 use the design review to decide which controls to go on testing. An inadequate design cannot manage its risk however well it is performed, so under Standard 14.2 the gap is already a potential finding. Testing both, the closest choice, asks for evidence the design review has already supplied.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: conclusions do need evidence, but for a badly designed control the design review supplies it. Perfect operation would still not manage the risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Risk does steer testing, but the weak control's risk is already established by its design gap. A sound design must still be shown to operate.
wrong_explanations.D: Findings are discussed with management, but that does not hold up the work. The sound control can be tested while the design gap is evaluated.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the weak control's risk is already shown by its design gap, and D, because discussing a finding with management does not hold up testing.
Final two: C beats A because the design review is the evidence for the weak control; testing its operation would add little to that conclusion.
Exam cue: design usually comes first, then operation. Test operation where the design could work; where it could not, report the design and size its effect.

questions.subtopic: 1C8 Control design, effectiveness and efficiency. Judging a nonfinancial control by its own objective
questions.question: A Zambian copper mine's gas checks before each shift fall within internal auditor Mwila Banda's engagement on underground operations. Which treatment of the checks is BEST?

options.A: Review their design and operation against the mine's output and cost targets
options.B: Review their design and operation against the aim of keeping workers safe
options.C: Test their operation, and take their design from the mine's engineers
options.D: Review their design, and take their operation from the supervisors' sign-offs

questions.key_concept: Nonfinancial controls get the same design and operation review as financial ones, judged against the objective each control exists to protect.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the gas checks are there to protect; that objective is the yardstick for their design and operation.
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary ties a control to the risk it manages and the objective it protects, with no limit to financial objectives, and Standard 13.4 has internal auditors use the criteria most relevant to what is being evaluated. Gas checks exist to keep workers safe, so their design and operation are judged against that aim. Output and cost targets, the closest choice, measure the mine's performance, not whether the checks manage their risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the scope is right, but the yardstick is not. A control is judged against the risk it manages; output and cost targets say nothing about gas.
wrong_explanations.C: Operation alone is half the review. Whether the checks would catch a gas build-up is the design question, and the engineers who set them are not an objective source.
wrong_explanations.D: A supervisor's sign-off is management's own statement that the checks were done. Operation is tested with evidence the auditor examines, as for any control.

tips: Eliminate: C, because design is part of the review and its owners are not an objective source, and D, because a sign-off is management's statement, not a test of operation.
Final two: B beats A because a control is judged against the risk it manages; gas checks protect workers, whatever the mine's output and cost targets say.
Exam cue: a control is defined by the risk it manages, not by whether money is involved. Judge a safety, quality or service control against its own objective.

questions.subtopic: 1C1 Organizational governance basics. The document that shows who covers each risk
questions.question: A Sri Lankan port's audit committee asks which team or outside body reviews each significant risk, and which risks nobody reviews. Which document should chief audit executive Nuwan Silva present to answer MOST directly?

options.A: The risk register
options.B: The internal audit plan
options.C: The assurance map
options.D: The risk and control matrix

questions.key_concept: An assurance map lines up significant risks with the internal and external providers that cover them, showing where coverage is missing or doubled.
questions.pre_read: Each planning document answers a different question. Which one is built around who gives assurance?
questions.correct_explanation: An assurance map sets the organization's significant risks beside every provider of assurance, inside and outside, so it shows at a glance where coverage overlaps and where there is none. Standard 9.5's considerations describe it as one way for the chief audit executive to coordinate coverage. The risk and control matrix, the closest choice, also starts from risks, but links them to objectives and controls, not to the parties who review them.

wrong_explanations.A: The risk register lists the risks with their ratings, owners and responses. It says who manages each risk, not who independently reviews it.
wrong_explanations.B: The plan shows only internal audit's own engagements for the period. Coverage by compliance, risk management and outside bodies does not appear in it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: a risk and control matrix links objectives, risks and the controls meant to manage them. It records controls, not which provider gives assurance over each risk.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the risk register records ratings, owners and responses and not reviewers, and B, because the internal audit plan lists one provider's work.
Final two: C beats D because the question is who covers each risk; an assurance map lines risks up with providers, a risk and control matrix with controls.
Exam cue: match the tool to the question asked. Risks by rating and owner: the register. Risks by control: the matrix. Risks by who gives assurance: the assurance map.

questions.subtopic: 1C1 Organizational governance basics. The Three Lines Model in a small organization
questions.question: An unregulated 40-person Samoan boatbuilder has no risk or compliance team: managers monitor their own risks; internal audit reports to the board. Which view by internal auditor Tala Leota fits the Three Lines Model BEST?

options.A: Sound: the model describes roles, and structure follows size and risks
options.B: Sound: the model is meant for organizations large enough for separate teams
options.C: Deficient: a second line is more objective when separate from operations
options.D: Deficient: managers who monitor their own risks give no assurance

questions.key_concept: The Three Lines Model describes roles, not departments. Whether separate second-line functions are needed depends on the organization's size and risks.
questions.pre_read: Does the model prescribe departments, or describe who owns risk, who supports and who assures?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on the Three Lines Model sets out roles, not an organization chart, and expects arrangements to differ between organizations. A small unregulated firm can leave monitoring with its managers unless its risks demand more; management sets up second-line roles, and the board decides whether the lines are established, expanded or combined. The closest choice treats separation, which makes an existing second-line role more objective, as a duty to create one.

wrong_explanations.B: The statement presents the model as fitting every organization. Size changes how the roles are arranged, not whether the model applies.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: separation does make a second line more objective than the first. But the model does not require every organization to set up such a team.
wrong_explanations.D: The model counts first-line supervision and monitoring among the sources of assurance. They are less objective than internal audit's work, which is why the board has both.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the model is meant for organizations of every size, and D, because first-line monitoring is part of the model, though less objective.
Final two: A beats C because the model describes roles and lets structure follow size and risk; separation adds objectivity only where a second-line role exists.
Exam cue: the Three Lines Model is not an organization chart. Ask whether risks are owned, overseen and independently assured, not how many departments exist.

questions.subtopic: 1C1 Organizational governance basics. Sharing the plan with another assurance provider
questions.question: A Belgian rail operator's compliance head, whose monitoring internal audit will assess this year, asks chief audit executive Lotte Maes to share the internal audit plan to align their reviews. What is Lotte's BEST response?

options.A: Withhold it: internal audit must stay independent of the areas it assesses
options.B: Withhold it: internal audit's scope must be free from interference
options.C: Share it once the board agrees: the plan must have board approval
options.D: Share it: the chief audit executive must coordinate with other providers

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive must coordinate with other assurance providers, including functions internal audit assesses. Independence rests on position and freedom from interference, not isolation.
questions.pre_read: What actually makes internal audit independent, and does sharing a plan touch any of it?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.5 requires the chief audit executive to coordinate with other providers of assurance, and its considerations give aligning the timing of planned work and access to each other's work programs as ways to do it. Sharing the plan applies that requirement. Independence comes from position and freedom from interference, and The IIA's 2026 Three Lines statement warns against reading it as isolation. Board approval, the closest choice, covers the plan's content, not coordinating it.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit assesses second-line work, but independence rests on its reporting line and freedom from interference. Coordination is required; aligning plans is one way to do it.
wrong_explanations.B: Freedom from interference means no one else sets internal audit's scope. Seeing the plan gives the compliance head information, not a say: the chief audit executive still decides.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the board approves the plan and significant changes to it. Sharing it changes nothing, and coordinating with other providers is the chief audit executive's own duty.

tips: Eliminate: A, because independence rests on position and freedom from interference, not distance, and B, because seeing the plan gives another team no say over scope.

Final two: D beats C because board approval covers the plan's content; coordinating with other providers is the chief audit executive's own duty; board approval of the plan is not a condition for sharing it.
Exam cue: independent does not mean isolated. On CIA questions the chief audit executive coordinates with other providers, even ones internal audit assesses, and still decides internal audit's scope.

questions.subtopic: 1C3 Ethics and compliance issues. Lawful conduct against the code
questions.question: A Mozambican telecom's code of conduct promises customers the best-fitting tariff; auditing network-repair tickets, internal auditor Zito Macamo reads the call-center head's lawful instruction to hide cheaper tariffs from callers. Which view is MOST accurate?

options.A: Not reportable: the instruction is lawful, so no requirement is broken
options.B: Not reportable: call-center conduct lies outside the engagement's scope
options.C: Reportable: misleading callers is discreditable behavior under the Standards
options.D: Reportable: the instruction goes against the telecom's ethical expectations

questions.key_concept: An ethics concern is measured against the organization's own ethical expectations. Lawful conduct, or conduct outside the engagement's scope, can still be reportable.
questions.pre_read: What is the yardstick for an ethics concern: the law, the scope, the Standards, or the organization's code?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.2 requires internal auditors to recognize conduct that goes against the organization's ethical expectations and to report it as policies and procedures direct. The code's promise to customers is such an expectation, and an order to hide cheaper tariffs breaks it. Scope, the closest choice, limits what an engagement sets out to test; the duty covers conduct identified anywhere in the organization. Lawfulness does not settle it either: law is a floor.

wrong_explanations.A: Law is the floor, not the test. Standard 1.2's duty turns on the organization's own ethical expectations, and Standard 1.3 adds a separate duty for legal violations.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: scope limits what the engagement sets out to test. The reporting duty covers conduct the internal auditor identifies anywhere in the organization, planned for or not.
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 1.3's examples of discreditable behavior, misleading others among them, govern internal auditors' own conduct. Staff are measured against the organization's own ethical expectations.

tips: Eliminate: A, because law is the floor and the test is the organization's own ethical expectations, and C, because the Standards' discreditable behavior list governs internal auditors, not staff.
Final two: D beats B because scope limits the planned testing, not the duty to report conduct that the internal auditor identifies while doing the work.
Exam cue: for an ethics concern ask one question: does the conduct go against what the organization expects of its people? Legality and scope do not settle it.

questions.subtopic: 1C4 Types of risk. The rating to compare with risk appetite
questions.question: An Angolan port's risk committee asks internal auditor Luísa Neto whether its risks are within the risk appetite. Which register figure is MOST relevant for Luísa to compare with the appetite?

options.A: The inherent risk rating
options.B: The residual risk rating
options.C: The target risk rating
options.D: The control effectiveness rating

questions.key_concept: Risk appetite and tolerance are compared with residual risk: the exposure left after the management actions already in place.
questions.pre_read: Each rating answers a different question. Which one says how much risk is carried today?
questions.correct_explanation: Risk appetite says how much risk, and of what kinds, the organization will take on, so it is set against the risk the port bears today: residual risk, the part of inherent risk left once management's actions are in place. The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management has internal audit check that what remains after management's responses sits within appetite and tolerance. A target rating, the closest choice, counts actions not yet taken.

wrong_explanations.A: Inherent risk counts none of management's actions. It shows where controls matter most, but the port does not bear that level while its controls work.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a target rating shows where planned actions should take the risk. Until those actions are in place, it describes an intention, not the risk borne today.
wrong_explanations.D: A control effectiveness rating says how well controls work, one input to residual risk. It is not a level of risk that can be set against appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A, because inherent risk leaves out everything management already does, and D, because a control effectiveness rating describes controls, not a level of risk.
Final two: B beats C because appetite is compared with the risk borne now; a target rating counts actions that are still only planned.
Exam cue: inherent risk shows where controls matter, residual risk shows what is borne now, target risk shows what is planned. Appetite and tolerance are compared with residual risk.

questions.subtopic: 1C4 Types of risk. Residual risk and the significance of a finding
questions.question: Internal auditor Mariana Solís finds a design gap in a Honduran exporter's customs-form check; a later control, tested and found effective, catches the same errors before filing. How should Mariana BEST judge the gap's significance?

options.A: By the errors that could still get through to a customs filing
options.B: By the errors the check would let through if it stood alone
options.C: By the cost of redesigning the check so that the gap closes
options.D: By the rating the check's manager gives the gap when asked

questions.key_concept: A finding's significance is judged by residual risk: likelihood and impact after the existing controls that work are counted.
questions.pre_read: Before rating a gap, ask what else already manages the same risk, and whether it works.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 has internal auditors judge a finding's significance by the likelihood and impact of the risk, and its considerations describe the method: take the controls already in place, check that each is adequate and works, and rate what they leave. A tested later control that stops the same errors lowers that risk. The closest choice measures the check as if it stood alone, ignoring a control that works.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: this sizes the risk as if no other control existed. Significance rests on likelihood and impact, and a working later control lowers the likelihood that errors are filed.
wrong_explanations.C: Cost against benefit is weighed when a recommendation or action plan is evaluated. It says what a remedy is worth, not how significant the gap is.
wrong_explanations.D: Management's input helps in estimating the effect, and the Standards ask for it. The judgment of significance stays with the internal auditor.

tips: Eliminate: C, because cost against benefit tests a remedy and not the gap's significance, and D, because management gives input while the internal auditor makes the judgment.
Final two: A beats B because significance follows the risk that remains with working controls counted; a tested later control changes the likelihood of harm.
Exam cue: a design gap is rated by residual risk, not on its own. Count every tested control that covers the same risk before you rate the finding.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. What enterprise risk management adds
questions.question: Each department of a Swedish paper group manages its own risks well, and the chief financial officer asks internal auditor Linnea Berg what enterprise risk management would add. Which answer is MOST accurate?

options.A: A risk function that maintains the framework and monitors chosen risks
options.B: Independent assurance that each department's risk responses are working
options.C: A single view of risks across departments for executives and the board
options.D: A yearly register of each department's risks, rated on one scale

questions.key_concept: Enterprise risk management joins separate risk efforts into one organization-wide view that leaders can act on; it does not replace the departments' own risk work.
questions.pre_read: Departments already manage their risks. What is still missing for the people who steer the whole organization?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management calls it an approach coordinated across the whole organization that does not replace the risk work departments already do. Its contribution is the joined-up view: executives and the board see every department's risks side by side and can decide where to take more risk and where less. A yearly register, the closest choice, is a record of one moment, which the statement sets apart from it.

wrong_explanations.A: A risk function supports enterprise risk management by keeping the framework and monitoring risks. It is a second-line role, not the approach itself, which managers at every level carry out.
wrong_explanations.B: Independent assurance over risk responses is what the internal audit function gives. Enterprise risk management is management's own process, which internal audit then assesses.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: one scale makes ratings comparable, but a yearly register is a static record. Enterprise risk management is continuous and feeds decisions at the top.

tips: Eliminate: B, because independent assurance comes from internal audit and not from management's own process, and A, because the risk function supports the approach and is not the approach.
Final two: C beats D because enterprise risk management is a continuing, organization-wide process that informs top-level decisions; a yearly register is a record.
Exam cue: enterprise risk management is not a department, an audit or a document. It is the organization-wide approach that joins up risk work for the board and executives.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. After the board decides on an accepted risk
questions.question: Chief audit executive Farida Rahimi escalated a Tajik power utility's acceptance of a single-supplier risk above its risk appetite; the board decided to keep carrying the risk. What is Farida's BEST course now?

options.A: Raise the risk again at each board meeting until it is reduced
options.B: Record the board's decision and treat the escalation as complete
options.C: Report the accepted risk to the utility's regulator
options.D: Withdraw the related finding from the engagement results

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive must communicate risk accepted above appetite or tolerance; resolving it is not that executive's job, and the board decides.
questions.pre_read: Where does the escalation ladder end, and who owns the decision at the top of it?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.5 gives the chief audit executive a duty to communicate: discuss risk accepted above appetite or tolerance with senior management, then the board if unresolved. The same requirement says resolving the risk is not that executive's responsibility; the considerations leave the response to the board and say discussions should be documented. No further step is set. Raising the risk at every meeting, the closest choice, turns informing the board into a campaign.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: persistence feels like professional courage, but the Standard asks the chief audit executive to communicate, not to resolve. The board has heard the matter and decided.
wrong_explanations.C: Reports to outside bodies are made where laws or regulations require them. Nothing here does; the board is the body with authority over this risk.
wrong_explanations.D: The board accepted the risk; it did not erase the gap. The finding stays in the engagement results, with the acceptance on record.

tips: Eliminate: C, because outside reporting follows a legal duty that is absent here, and D, because acceptance of a risk does not remove the finding from the results.
Final two: B beats A because the chief audit executive must communicate the accepted risk, not resolve it; once the board has decided, the escalation has done its job.
Exam cue: for risk accepted above appetite, the ladder ends at the board, which decides. An ethics breach by senior management differs: there, internal auditors should follow up on the action taken.

questions.subtopic: 1C6 Risk management across the organization. Where advice fits better than assurance
questions.question: Chief audit executive Aya Koné is weighing internal audit's risk management work at four subsidiaries of an Ivorian cashew group. At which one does advisory work, more than assurance, fit BEST?

options.A: The one that is building its first risk management process this year
options.B: The one with an embedded process and a run of unreported incidents
options.C: The one whose capable risk function already monitors every unit
options.D: The one whose regulator requires yearly assurance on risk management

questions.key_concept: Internal audit's mix of advice and assurance on risk management follows maturity: advice may lead while the process is built, assurance once it is established.
questions.pre_read: What does a risk management process that is still being built need most from internal audit?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management lets the mix of services follow maturity. While a process is still taking shape, advisory work may take the larger share, helping to build it, provided internal audit can still assure it independently afterward. The closest choice also looks like a call for help, but there the statement leans the other way: for an embedded process, and where incidents raise concerns, it says assurance may come first.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: unreported incidents in an embedded process are a reason to test whether it works. The statement says assurance may take priority where such concerns arise.
wrong_explanations.C: Where a capable second line monitors well, the statement points to coordinating assurance with it and relying on its work where that is justified, not to more advice.
wrong_explanations.D: The regulator asks for assurance, which advice does not give. Engagements that laws or regulations require are among those the chief audit executive should consider for the plan.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a capable second line points to coordinated assurance and reliance, and D, because assurance that a regulator requires cannot be replaced by advice.
Final two: A beats B because advice may lead while a process is being built; incidents in an embedded process are a reason to test whether it works.
Exam cue: the mix of advice and assurance follows maturity, as a may and not a rule. Young process: advice may lead, with later assurance kept possible. Established process: assurance may lead.

questions.subtopic: 1C6 Risk management across the organization. The missing yardstick in the design
questions.question: Internal auditor Jelena Ilić lists four features of risk management at a Serbian furniture maker. Which one should Jelena report as the MAIN gap in its design?

options.A: Units rate the risks that they themselves own
options.B: The board has no separate risk committee
options.C: Internal audit facilitated the units' risk-rating workshops
options.D: The board has not established a risk appetite

questions.key_concept: Sound risk management design includes an established risk appetite; the board establishes it, and internal audit gives assurance on whether it exists and is used.
questions.pre_read: Which of these is a missing foundation, and which are ordinary ways of organizing risk work?
questions.correct_explanation: A risk appetite tells managers how much risk, and of which kinds, they may carry; risk management designed without one has no yardstick. The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management puts an established appetite and tolerance among the first things internal audit gives assurance on, and both 2026 statements have the board establish the appetite. A separate risk committee, the closest choice, is one way to organize oversight, not a requirement.

wrong_explanations.A: Managers own their risks, so rating them is their job. Internal audit assesses whether those ratings are reliable and consistent; second-line roles may challenge them.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a board may oversee risk itself or through a committee. The IIA's 2026 statements say they prescribe no organizational structure, so its absence alone is no gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Facilitating risk workshops is advisory work that the 2026 statement on enterprise risk management names. Managers still own the ratings, so it is not a design gap.

tips: Eliminate: A, because managers own their risks and rate them, and C, because facilitating workshops is advisory work that leaves the ratings with managers.
Final two: D beats B because a board can oversee risk without a separate committee, but without an established appetite nobody knows how much risk is acceptable.
Exam cue: when judging the design of risk management, look first for the yardstick: has the board established a risk appetite that decisions can be measured against?

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. When management should propose the fix
questions.question: Internal auditor Ayesha Malik finds bag weights outside limits at a Pakistani cement plant, whose engineers are still testing whether scales or valves are at fault. Which course on corrective action fits the Standards BEST?

options.A: Recommend replacing scales and valves, so that either cause is covered
options.B: Request an action plan from management, with an owner and a date
options.C: Agree a repair with management now, with an owner and a date
options.D: Report the finding once the engineers have settled on a repair

questions.key_concept: For each finding the internal auditor chooses among recommending, requesting management's action plan, or agreeing actions jointly; the facts decide which fits.
questions.pre_read: Must the internal auditor always be the one who names the fix?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.4 gives internal auditors three routes for each finding: develop recommendations, ask management for an action plan, or settle the actions together with management. None is ranked above the others; the facts choose. Here those able to trace the cause are still tracing it, so a plan from management, judged on whether it deals with that cause, fits. Agreeing a repair now, the closest choice, commits both sides to a guess.

wrong_explanations.A: A recommendation should address the root cause at a cost in proportion to the risk. Replacing both parts to cover either cause buys a repair that may be half unneeded.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: agreeing actions with management is a valid route, but an action should address the root cause, and that is not yet known.
wrong_explanations.D: The gap exists whatever repair is chosen. Findings are discussed with management promptly and reported; the action plan can follow the engineers' tests.

tips: Eliminate: A, because replacing both parts sets cost against benefit aside while the cause is unknown, and D, because a finding is not held back until a remedy is chosen.
Final two: B beats C because an agreed action must address the root cause; while the cause is still being traced, management's own plan is the fitting route.
Exam cue: a recommendation is one of three routes, not a duty. When management is better placed to find the fix, ask for its action plan and assess it.

questions.subtopic: 1C8 Control design, effectiveness and efficiency. When control design is evaluated
questions.question: An engagement supervisor at a Barbadian credit union tells internal auditor Kemar Brown that the Standards require control design to be evaluated before any test of how a control operates. Which reply is MOST accurate?

options.A: They do: a design conclusion must appear in the approved work program
options.B: They do: testing a control of unjudged design wastes audit effort
options.C: They do not: design may be judged in planning or alongside testing
options.D: They do not: design may be left aside unless operating tests fail

questions.key_concept: Judging control design before testing operation is a sensible option, not a requirement: the considerations let it happen in planning, later, or alongside testing.
questions.pre_read: Is design-before-operation a requirement, or good practice the considerations describe?
questions.correct_explanation: No requirement fixes the order. Standard 13.6's considerations treat planning as one possible time for the design review, useful because it shows which key controls deserve testing, and add that the right moment varies with the engagement: later, or while operating tests are performed. The closest choice gives a sound reason to judge design early, the cost of fully testing a control that is not adequately designed, but a sound reason is not a requirement.

wrong_explanations.A: The work program must name criteria, tasks, methods and the auditors assigned. The design review should be documented there or in a workpaper, but no requirement makes it come first.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: due professional care weighs the cost of fully testing poorly designed controls, a good reason to judge design early. That makes the order sensible, not mandatory.
wrong_explanations.D: The considerations let the timing of the design evaluation vary; none makes it optional. A control performed faithfully can still fail to manage its risk.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the work program's required content does not include a design conclusion, and D, because the considerations vary only the timing of the design evaluation and never make it optional.
Final two: C beats B because the cost argument is a good reason to judge design early, while the considerations leave the timing to the engagement.
Exam cue: when a question says the Standards require something, check whether the rule sits in the requirements or the considerations. Design first is a sensible option, not a must.

questions.subtopic: 1C1 Organizational governance basics. When the external auditor's tests serve another objective
questions.question: A Jordanian dairy's external auditor tests payables only for its financial statement opinion; a board member proposes dropping internal audit's planned review of purchasing efficiency. What is chief audit executive Rania Haddad's BEST response?

options.A: Advise keeping it: the external auditor's independence is unproven
options.B: Advise keeping it: the external audit's tests serve another objective
options.C: Accept dropping it: changes to the plan are the board's to approve
options.D: Advise deferring it until the external auditor's results are evaluated

questions.key_concept: External auditors serve outside parties within a scope set by law. Reliance needs work aimed at the same objectives, not merely the same transactions.
questions.pre_read: Before relying on another provider, ask what its work is for, not only which records it touches.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.5 has the chief audit executive coordinate with outside providers and consider relying on their work, and The IIA's 2026 Three Lines statement places external auditors outside the three lines, serving outside parties within a legal scope. Tests built for a financial statement opinion say nothing about purchasing efficiency, so the review should stay in the plan. The closest choice would suit an unclear overlap; here the stem already shows the objectives differ.

wrong_explanations.A: Independence is one factor when weighing reliance, but nothing here puts it in doubt. The deciding fact is that the external tests serve another objective.
wrong_explanations.C: The board does approve the plan and significant changes to it, but the chief audit executive must discuss such changes with it, which means giving advice, not simply agreeing.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: evaluating another provider's work comes before relying on it. Here nothing needs evaluating, because the external auditor's tests were never aimed at purchasing efficiency.

tips: Eliminate: A, because nothing here puts the external auditor's independence in doubt, and C, because the board's approval follows the chief audit executive's advice rather than replacing it.
Final two: B beats D because the stem already shows the external tests serve a different objective, so there is no work to evaluate for reliance.
Exam cue: when another provider's work is offered as a substitute, compare objectives first. The same transactions do not mean the same assurance.

questions.subtopic: 1C3 Ethics and compliance issues. Ethics risks inside an ordinary engagement
questions.question: Internal auditor Hamid Alaoui is planning a Moroccan port's procurement assurance engagement; next year's plan holds a separate ethics program engagement. How should Hamid BEST treat the risk of buyers accepting supplier gifts?

options.A: Leave it to next year's engagement on the ethics program
options.B: Refer it to the ethics officer, who runs the gifts policy
options.C: Cover it if the procurement managers first agree to widen the scope
options.D: Weigh it among this engagement's risks and the controls over it

questions.key_concept: Plan-level coverage of the ethics program does not replace engagement-level care: each engagement should weigh its own ethics-related risks and controls, fraud included.
questions.pre_read: Does a later ethics engagement remove ethics risks from this engagement, or only add a wider look?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.2's considerations ask internal auditors to weigh ethics-related risks and controls in each engagement, and Standard 13.2 requires every engagement risk assessment to identify the activity's significant risks and to consider fraud. Gifts that sway buyers raise both concerns in procurement. The closest choice relies on the plan's coverage of the ethics program, which Standard 9.4 requires the plan to consider; that wider review does not take the risk out of this engagement.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the plan must consider coverage of the ethics program, and next year's engagement does that. It does not remove a risk that sits inside this year's procurement work.
wrong_explanations.B: Management does own the gifts policy and its enforcement. Internal audit still assesses the risk and the controls over it in its own engagement, then reports what it finds.
wrong_explanations.C: Scope agreed with the requesting party fits advisory work. In an assurance engagement the internal auditors set the objectives and scope mainly themselves, from their risk assessment.

tips: Eliminate: B, because management owning the policy does not stop internal audit assessing the risk, and C, because scope set by agreement belongs to advisory work, not assurance.
Final two: D beats A because plan-level coverage of the ethics program is wider work; it does not take an ethics risk out of the engagement where it sits.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a later or separate engagement rarely removes a significant risk from the one being planned. Assess the risk where it arises.

questions.subtopic: 1C4 Types of risk. A control offered as a reason to cut inherent risk
questions.question: At an Ecuadorian shrimp packer, internal auditor Lucía Paredes rates inherent risk of uncertified shipments high; the export manager wants it lowered because a new system now blocks them. Which response is BEST?

options.A: Keep it: the block belongs in the residual rating once tested
options.B: Lower it: management's view of the risks should inform the rating
options.C: Lower it: the block has stopped every uncertified shipment so far
options.D: Keep it: the block has not yet been tested

questions.key_concept: Inherent risk is rated as if management had done nothing. Any control belongs in residual risk, which the auditor rates after evaluating that control.
questions.pre_read: Sort what the manager offers: facts about the risk itself, or something management does about it?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary defines inherent risk as the exposure with no management action counted, and residual risk as what remains once actions are in place. A system block is such an action, so it can lower residual risk after Lucía judges its design and operation, as Standard 14.3's considerations describe. The closest choice is sound when management's input concerns the risk itself, such as volumes; here the input is a control.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Standard 13.2's considerations do ask for management's input on risks and controls. Input about a control changes the residual rating, not the inherent one.
wrong_explanations.C: A record of blocked shipments is evidence that the control works. That evidence matters when rating residual risk; inherent risk leaves every control out.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing matters for residual risk. Even a tested block would leave the inherent rating where it is, because inherent risk counts no management action.

tips: Eliminate: C, because evidence that a control works feeds the residual rating, and D, because even a tested control leaves inherent risk unchanged.
Final two: A beats B because management's input is weighed where it belongs: a point about a control moves residual risk, not inherent risk.
Exam cue: when anyone argues an inherent rating down by pointing to a control, the control goes into residual risk instead.

questions.subtopic: 1C4 Types of risk. The risk type and a finding's weight
questions.question: A Fijian bank's board accepts some credit losses but no sanctions breaches; internal auditor Mere Vosa finds equally likely gaps in loan approvals and sanctions screening, each risking $40,000. How should Mere BEST rank them?

options.A: Equally: the two gaps share the same likelihood and impact
options.B: Loan gap first: lending is the main source of the bank's income
options.C: Screening gap first: far less of that risk type is acceptable
options.D: Equally, until managers give their view of each gap's impact

questions.key_concept: Significance weighs nature as well as size: where the board's appetite differs by type of risk, the same sum can matter more in one type.
questions.pre_read: Two gaps cost the same. What else about each risk could make one weigh more?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 requires significance to rest on likelihood and impact; its considerations add risk tolerance and other factors important to the organization, and the glossary counts a matter's nature as well as its size. Risk appetite covers types of risk as well as amounts, and this board accepts no sanctions breaches, so that gap ranks first. The closest choice stops at the two required factors.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: likelihood and impact must be weighed, and here they match. Significance also weighs the nature of each matter and how much of each type the board accepts.
wrong_explanations.B: Factors important to the organization can count, but the board has said directly how much of each risk it will bear. Credit losses sit inside that appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: Management's input helps estimate the size of an exposure, and here the sums are already known. The board's appetite settles the ranking without waiting.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the board's stated appetite outweighs a general view of what matters most, and D, because management's input refines a size the stem already gives.
Final two: C beats A because likelihood and impact are where significance starts; the board's appetite for each type of risk then separates two equal sums.
Exam cue: when two findings look equal in money, check the appetite or tolerance for each type of risk before ranking them.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. An action plan that keeps slipping
questions.question: Follow-up shows an Estonian shipper's fix for a risk above appetite is nine months late; its logistics manager moved the date twice without consulting internal audit. What should chief audit executive Kadri Tamm do FIRST?

options.A: Raise the delay with the manager and agree an updated plan
options.B: Discuss the delay with senior management as risk accepted above appetite
options.C: Keep tracking the fix until the manager's latest date has passed
options.D: Escalate the delay to the board, which decides on accepted risk

questions.key_concept: Stalled action can amount to accepting a risk; before senior management hears it, the chief audit executive should raise it with the responsible manager.
questions.pre_read: A late action plan: is it still routine follow-up, or has it become risk acceptance? And who hears about it first?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 15.2 has internal auditors get management's explanation for missed dates and tell the chief audit executive, who judges whether delay amounts to accepting the risk. Standard 11.5's considerations then take the concern to the responsible manager, to agree an updated plan, before senior management or the board. Nobody has yet put the delay to this manager, so that comes first; the senior management requirement applies if it fails.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: once the chief audit executive concludes the risk was accepted, senior management must hear it. The considerations first send it to the manager, whom nobody has yet asked.
wrong_explanations.C: Confirming that agreed actions are carried out is the normal follow-up duty. Nine months and two moved dates make waiting longer too weak a response.
wrong_explanations.D: The board decides only after senior management has failed to resolve the matter. Going straight to it skips two steps.

tips: Eliminate: C, because repeated delay is a reason to act on the risk, not to keep waiting, and D, because the board is the last step, after senior management.
Final two: A beats B because the considerations take a stalled plan to the responsible manager before senior management; the requirement starts when that fails.
Exam cue: for accepted risk, read the order: responsible management, then senior management, then the board. FIRST usually points to the earliest step not yet taken.

questions.subtopic: 1C6 Risk management across the organization. A register that missed a new strategy
questions.question: Chief audit executive Jón Einarsson relies on an Icelandic seafood exporter's risk register, having judged its process effective; since then the board approved a fish-farming venture, which the register omits. Which plan step is BEST?

options.A: Rely on the register and cover the venture in next year's plan
options.B: Fill the register's gap so the plan can keep relying on it
options.C: Stop using the register and rebuild the whole organizationwide assessment
options.D: Assess the venture's risks and recheck reliance on the register

questions.key_concept: Reliance on management's risk information holds only while the process keeps pace with strategy; a venture missing from the register needs internal audit's own assessment.
questions.pre_read: A process judged effective last time: does that judgment still cover risks the process has not yet caught?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4 requires a plan based on the chief audit executive's own documented risk assessment, kept up to date as the business changes. Its considerations allow reliance on management's risk information only when the risk management process is effective, and call for reliance to be reevaluated. The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management has assurance test whether risk identification is complete and in line with strategy. The closest choice was right before the venture.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: reliance suits a process judged effective. But the plan must change as risks change, and a register that missed an approved venture no longer earns reliance unchecked.
wrong_explanations.B: Management keeps its own register. Filling it in would be an expanded role that should have board approval and safeguards (The IIA's 2026 ERM statement).
wrong_explanations.C: Discarding the register suits a process shown to be unreliable throughout. One missed venture calls for rechecking reliance, not throwing out every rating the process produced.

tips: Eliminate: B, because maintaining management's register would expand internal audit's role, and C, because reliance is reevaluated for what changed, and one omission does not show the whole process unreliable.
Final two: D beats A because the plan must change as risks change, and reliance on management's risk information rests on a process that has kept pace with strategy.
Exam cue: after a strategic change, check any earlier reliance on management's risk information against the new risks before the plan uses it.

questions.subtopic: 1C6 Risk management across the organization. A second-line rating internal audit disputes
questions.question: A Slovenian insurer's risk function rates cyber risk green for a combined assurance report; internal audit found major gaps, and the risk head will not move. What is chief audit executive Ana Kovač's BEST course?

options.A: Hold the report until the two functions agree on one rating
options.B: Show both ratings, keeping internal audit's view independent
options.C: Use internal audit's rating, as the line with most independence
options.D: Use the risk function's rating, as the line that owns the rating

questions.key_concept: Combined reporting does not blend away disagreement: internal audit keeps its own conclusion and draws attention to first- or second-line information its evidence contradicts.
questions.pre_read: Coordination aims at one coherent picture. What happens when two providers' evidence points different ways?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.5 leaves the chief audit executive responsible for internal audit's own conclusions. The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management adds that, even in integrated assurance, the chief audit executive must keep questioning or drawing attention to first- or second-line information that is wrong, incomplete or not to be trusted. Showing both ratings does that and keeps management's view on record. The closest choice fits before discussion; here discussion has already failed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 8.1's considerations say a disagreement should typically be discussed first. That has happened, and waiting for agreement would keep a disputed rating from the board.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit's independence lets it decline to rely on another provider. It does not let internal audit rewrite the risk function's own rating in a joint report.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk function does own its rating. Printing it alone would pass on information that internal audit's evidence shows to be unreliable, with no challenge.

tips: Eliminate: C, because independence lets internal audit decline to rely on others, not overwrite their view, and D, because owning a rating does not make it reliable.
Final two: B beats A because the discussion has already taken place; holding the report would delay the board's view of a disputed risk.
Exam cue: in coordinated or combined reporting, internal audit keeps its own conclusion. Disagreement is shown to the board, not hidden or averaged away.

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. A board approval in the risk and control matrix
questions.question: A Vietnamese port operator's board must approve any contract above $5 million before it is signed. How should internal auditor Nguyen Thi Lan BEST record this approval in a risk and control matrix?

options.A: Not a control: controls are designed and run by management
options.B: A detective control: the board reviews each contract's terms
options.C: A preventive control: it stops unapproved contracts going ahead
options.D: Not a control: it is a governance process the board directs

questions.key_concept: A control is any action by management, the board or others that manages risk. An approval needed before commitment works as a preventive control.
questions.pre_read: Who can perform a control? And does this approval act before or after the contract exists?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary defines a control as any action taken by management, the board or other parties to manage risk, so a board approval qualifies. It acts before the contract binds the port, which makes it preventive; Standard 13.2's considerations list preventive, detective, directive and corrective as the types a matrix may record. The closest choice reflects the Three Lines Model, where management designs and runs most controls, but the definition is wider.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: in the Three Lines Model management designs and operates processes and controls. The glossary still counts actions by the board and other parties as controls.
wrong_explanations.B: A review of completed transactions detects problems after the event. This approval happens before signing, so it stops an unwanted contract rather than finding one.
wrong_explanations.D: Board approvals are part of governance, and that does not stop them being controls. Governance and control overlap: the board's own actions can manage risk.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a step that happens before signing stops the risk rather than finding it, and D, because a governance process can also be a control.
Final two: C beats A because the glossary counts actions by the board and other parties as controls, while the Three Lines Model describes who runs most of them.
Exam cue: classify a control by when it acts, and do not rule one out because the board or an outside party performs it.

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. A costly control that also meets a legal duty
questions.question: Romanian law requires a controlled-drug register; at one pharmacy chain it costs more than the theft it deters, so the operations head plans to scrap it. How should internal auditor Ioana Pop BEST assess this?

options.A: Sound: a control should not cost more than the risk it manages
options.B: Sound, once the drug regulator is told the register will stop
options.C: Unsound: detective controls should stay beside preventive ones
options.D: Unsound: the theft figures leave out its legal purpose

questions.key_concept: A control can serve several objectives at once. One that a law requires serves compliance, so theft figures alone cannot justify removing it.
questions.pre_read: Before judging a control too costly, list every objective it serves.
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary counts as a control any action that helps meet objectives, and compliance with law is one of them; Standard 9.1 lists it among the key risk areas. The register keeps the chain within a law that requires it, so its value is not measured by theft deterred, and scrapping it would breach that law. The closest choice applies a sound cost test to one objective only.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: weighing cost against benefit is sound, but here only theft is counted. The register also keeps the chain within the law that requires it.
wrong_explanations.B: Disclosures that law requires must be made, but telling a regulator does not make it lawful to stop keeping a register the law requires.
wrong_explanations.C: Mixing control types is sound design in general. The stem gives no preventive control; what decides this case is the register's legal purpose.

tips: Eliminate: B, because telling the regulator does not make dropping a required register lawful, and C, because the stem turns on the register's legal purpose, not on the mix of control types.
Final two: D beats A because a cost test that counts only theft leaves out the register's legal purpose, and scrapping the register would breach the law.
Exam cue: when a control looks too costly, list every objective it serves. A control that a law requires is not dropped on cost grounds while the law stands.

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. A management fix that leaves risk above tolerance
questions.question: Internal auditor Gor Petrosyan recommended an Armenian telecom block duplicate refunds in its system; the billing manager prefers a monthly review that Gor finds leaves losses above tolerance. What is Gor's BEST course?

options.A: Accept the review and confirm later that it is in place
options.B: Keep the recommendation and follow the methodology for disagreements
options.C: Accept the review, as management owns the choice of remedy
options.D: Keep the recommendation and take it to the board as accepted risk

questions.key_concept: Management may choose its own remedy if it brings the risk within tolerance. If it does not, the disagreement goes through the established methodology.
questions.pre_read: Management's alternative fix: is it satisfactory, judged against the risk tolerance?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.4 requires actions that bring risk to an acceptable level and, when auditors and management disagree on recommendations, an established methodology that lets both state their case. Its considerations judge actions against the organization's risk tolerance. Management may pick its own remedy, but this one leaves losses above tolerance, so Gor keeps the recommendation. The closest choice is right when internal auditors agree the alternative is satisfactory or better.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: management's alternative is tracked if internal auditors agree it is satisfactory or better than the original. This review leaves losses above the tolerance.
wrong_explanations.C: Management does choose and implement remedies, but an action that leaves risk above tolerance does not resolve the finding, so the disagreement is not over.
wrong_explanations.D: Risk accepted above tolerance reaches the board only after the chief audit executive has discussed it with senior management and it stays unresolved.

tips: Eliminate: C, because management's choice of remedy still has to bring the risk within tolerance, and D, because the board comes last, after senior management.
Final two: B beats A because an alternative is tracked if internal auditors agree it is satisfactory or better than the original; this one leaves losses above tolerance.
Exam cue: when management offers a different fix, test it against the risk tolerance. Within tolerance or better, track it; otherwise the disagreement methodology applies.

questions.subtopic: 1C8 Control design, effectiveness and efficiency. A control in place for half the period
questions.question: Internal auditor Mynor Pérez's assurance engagement covers a Guatemalan exporter's full year: its required invoice check stopped in January; Mynor's tests show management's automated replacement has worked since July. Which conclusion BEST meets the Standards?

options.A: Effective: the automated check now works as it was designed
options.B: Not effective: the replacement has not yet run for a full year
options.C: Not effective for the year; the replacement has worked since July
options.D: Effective, as no invoice errors were found from January to June

questions.key_concept: An assurance conclusion judges the scope's whole period, and the final communication acknowledges fixes management has already made, such as a replacement control.
questions.pre_read: The scope is a full year; the required control existed for half of it. What one judgment fits, and what must it acknowledge?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.5 requires an assurance conclusion on control effectiveness, and the scope sets its period (Standard 13.3), here the full year. The required check was missing from January to June, so the year is not effective. Standard 15.1 also requires the final communication to acknowledge actions management has already taken on a finding, so the replacement working since July belongs in it. The closest choice reaches the verdict but omits that acknowledgment.

wrong_explanations.A: The automated check does work, and that must be acknowledged. The scope is the whole year, though, and half of it had no check.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the verdict is right, but the year fails for the six months with no check, and Standard 15.1 requires acknowledging the replacement management already put in place.
wrong_explanations.D: Clean invoices show an outcome, not that a control ran. With no check from January to June, there was no control to judge effective.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the scope is the whole year, not only the months since July, and D, because error-free invoices cannot show that an absent control operated.
Final two: C beats B because both rightly fail the year, but only C acknowledges the working replacement, as Standard 15.1 requires for actions management has already taken on a finding.
Exam cue: give one judgment for the scope's full period, and acknowledge any fix management has already made, such as a control replaced partway through.

questions.subtopic: 1C8 Control design, effectiveness and efficiency. No framework and no criteria yet
questions.question: A Lesotho water charity has adopted no internal control framework, and internal auditor Palesa Mokoena judges its grants criteria inadequate. Before assurance testing of grants, what should Palesa do FIRST?

options.A: Discuss with senior management which criteria the grants review will use
options.B: Apply a recognized control framework, since such frameworks are adequate criteria
options.C: Recommend that the charity adopt a framework before testing begins
options.D: Turn the engagement into advisory work, which may need no criteria

questions.key_concept: Without adequate criteria, internal auditors must identify suitable ones by discussion with the board or senior management; a recognized framework is a common source.
questions.pre_read: The criteria are judged inadequate. Which step is required, and which are only options the considerations allow?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.4 requires internal auditors to use the board's and senior management's criteria when adequate and, when they fall short, to settle suitable criteria by talking with the board or senior management. A recognized internal control framework is one authoritative source to propose. The closest choice picks a fair source but skips the required discussion. The considerations also allow recommending that management adopt criteria, or moving to advisory work, but neither comes first.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: authoritative frameworks are among the adequate criteria the considerations name. The requirement is still to settle criteria through discussion, not to impose them.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal auditors may recommend that management implement suitable criteria. Holding the engagement for a formal adoption is not required, and criteria can be agreed now.
wrong_explanations.D: A talk about missing criteria may lead to advisory work, but the plan calls for assurance, and that talk has not yet happened.

tips: Eliminate: C, because recommending adoption is an option that need not hold up the engagement, and D, because any switch to advisory work would come out of the discussion about criteria, not before it.
Final two: A beats B because a framework is a good source of criteria, but the Standards require criteria to be identified through discussion when none are adequate.
Exam cue: separate the must from the mays. Discussing criteria is required; where they come from, and what follows, are options.

questions.subtopic: 1C3 Ethics and compliance issues. A voluntary code made binding by a contract
questions.question: A Zimbabwean cooperative's counsel confirms no law binds it to a governance code, but its bank made the code's board committee rules a loan condition. How should internal auditor Tendai Moyo BEST treat those rules?

options.A: As good practice, since a loan condition is not a law
options.B: As a legal requirement, since the code is recognized nationally
options.C: As a requirement, binding through a contract the cooperative signed
options.D: As criteria once the cooperative's board adopts the code as its policy

questions.key_concept: Compliance covers contracts as well as laws, so a voluntary code becomes a requirement when a contract the organization signed imposes it.
questions.pre_read: No law imposes the code. Is a loan condition a requirement, and what does compliance cover?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary counts contracts, alongside laws, regulations and the organization's own policies, among the requirements that compliance covers. A loan condition is a term of the loan contract, so the code's committee rules bind the cooperative, and Tendai treats them as compliance criteria. The closest choice reads only law as binding; it fits an organization that nothing obliges to follow the code.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a code that nothing binds an organization to is a benchmark. A loan condition is a contract term, and contracts are among the requirements compliance covers.
wrong_explanations.B: Being recognized nationally does not make a code law. Its rules bind an organization when a law, a regulator or, as here, a contract imposes them.
wrong_explanations.D: Board adoption would make the code the cooperative's own policy, but the loan agreement already binds the cooperative, whatever its board decides.

tips: Eliminate: B, because national recognition does not turn a code into law, and D, because the loan contract binds the cooperative without any board adoption.
Final two: C beats A because compliance covers contracts as well as laws, so a code that a loan condition imposes is a requirement, not just good practice.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, ask what binds this organization: law, regulation, contract or its own policy. Any of them can turn guidance into a compliance requirement.

questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. Unclear decision rights behind a purchase
questions.question: A Namibian port's delegation policy is silent on software, so its IT and finance heads each assumed the other approved a $2 million system. What MAIN weakness should internal auditor Selma Nangolo report?

options.A: Decision rights: no approver is assigned for this kind of purchase
options.B: Operation: the finance head's sign-off on the purchase was skipped
options.C: Risk information: the heads did not see the system's risks first
options.D: Challenge: no second-line review questioned the purchase beforehand

questions.key_concept: Decision-making processes shape control: when no approver is assigned for a kind of decision, approvals fall through the gap, a root cause in design.
questions.pre_read: Did any rule require the finance head's approval? If not, can a missing approval be an operating failure?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.1 requires the chief audit executive to consider how the organization makes decisions and structures its functions. Here the policy named no approver for software, so each head assumed the other had approved: a gap in decision rights, which is the root cause Standard 14.3 asks auditors to identify. The closest choice calls it a skipped sign-off, but no rule required one.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a skipped sign-off is an operating failure when a rule requires it. No rule required the finance head's approval, so the gap is in decision rights.
wrong_explanations.C: Missing risk information weakens decisions made without it. Here no one with authority made the decision at all, which comes before what the heads knew.
wrong_explanations.D: Second-line challenge matters where decisions call for it. Here no approver was assigned, so no one with authority made a decision for challenge to question.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the facts show no authorized person decided, so what the heads knew comes second, and D, because challenge needs a decision to question.
Final two: A beats B because an operating failure needs a required step that was skipped; where the policy names no approver, the root cause is the missing decision right.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, before calling a gap an operating failure, check that a rule required the step. No rule points to a design or governance gap.
